Schedule technical deep dive with Elmwood infra team next week (Ravi)

action_items: Owner: Maya Chen; Item: Share Private/VPC deployment runbook and security checklist; Due: 2026-06-29
Owner: Liam O'Connor; Item: Send VPC CIDRs, subnets, peering constraints, and current Transit Gateway setup; Due: 2026-06-28

summary: Initial discovery on Elmwood's requirements for a Private (VPC) deployment of Redwood. Primary concerns: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, region constraints, CIDR overlap, cross-account peering, egress/Audit/network path, KMS integration. Next step is technical deep dive and sharing runbook + network diagram.
transcript: [00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. we got ravi from our systems team, he will do the deep infra Qs. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Ava Martinez: good thanks. excited to get into this. we've been evaluating hosted APIs but have a lot of compliance constraints so private deployment seems likely.

[00:22] Ravi Patel: great, quick agenda — collect your constraints (networking, regions, security), share how our Private option works at a high level, and identify any red flags for a pilot. sound good?

[00:31] Liam O'Connor: yes. i'll jump in with network. we run multiple AWS accounts, we have an EKS control plane in us-east-1 and some data in eu-west-1. primary question is how Redwood will connect — VPC peering, privatelink, or transit gateway?
[00:45] Priya Kumar: and from security, we need KMS integration for keys, audit logs retained 1 year, and traffic not leaving our VPC. also SOC2 type 2 is required, and SSO via our SAML idp.

[01:05] Maya Chen: perfect — that maps to common asks. quick overview: Redwood Private can be deployed into your VPCs in two modes: (1) private endpoints / PrivateLink (we expose an interface endpoint in your account), or (2) we run the Redwood runtime in your VPC under a customer-managed stack (we can provide an AMI/container image). For many customers we offer a hybrid: control plane in a private, customer-facing plane with data path pinned to your VPC so tokens don't traverse public internet.

[01:35] Liam O'Connor: ok, in our case cross-account peering is tricky — security doesn't like long-lived peering relationships. we'd prefer an interface VPC endpoint or transit gateway attachment. any preference?

[01:47] Ravi Patel: both are workable. PrivateLink (interface ENIs) is good for avoiding peering and works cross-account, but it limits some L4 visibility and has ENI-level security group constraints. Transit Gateway is more flexible for complex topologies but requires TGW attachments and additional cost and routing. we typically recommend PrivateLink for standard API access and TGW when customers need broad network reachability across many accounts and on-prem connectivity.
[02:12] Ava Martinez: how about region coverage? we need eu-west-1 for GDPR and us-east-1 for latency to our app. can Redwood run in multiple regions for the same deployment?

[02:22] Maya Chen: yes — Private can be deployed per-region. you can pin a model deployment to a region. we can set up regional endpoints in us-east-1 and eu-west-1; data residency policies can be enforced at the deployment level. small caveat: model replication across regions will affect cost and capacity planning.
[02:41] Liam O'Connor: CIDR overlap is a concern — we have a 10.0.0.0/16 across accounts in many cases. how do you handle collisions?

[02:49] Ravi Patel: we ask for your VPC CIDRs and suggest a placement. for PrivateLink there is no peering so less collision risk because endpoints are in your VPC subnets. for peering/TGW we do need non-overlapping ranges. if you have overlaps, options are NAT/proxying, or put the Redwood runtime into a different account with non-overlapping ranges and use TGW routing. we'll need your network diagram to advise precisely.
[03:15] Priya Kumar: what about egress — are there any outbound calls from the runtime to Redwood-managed services? we need all egress to be auditable and go through our proxies.

[03:25] Ravi Patel: good question. in a full Private deployment, the runtime can be configured to use your egress via NAT or your egress proxies. default control-plane telemetry can be disabled or routed through your VPC. for hosted control plane variants, there may be occasional calls for updates, but we support an air-gapped/managed control plane for customers that require zero outbound. we'll capture the options in the runbook.
[03:50] Ava Martinez: KMS — we require that encryption keys are customer-managed and we control key rotation. can Redwood use our KMS or HSM?

[03:58] Maya Chen: yes we integrate with customer KMS for data at rest keys and can support customer-managed keys (CMK) in AWS KMS. for HSM/bring-your-own, we have options via partner integrations; we'll need to map exact secrets workflow in the technical deep dive.
[04:12] Liam O'Connor: certificate management for TLS? we'll terminate at our ALB. we don't want Redwood managing public certs in our account.

[04:20] Ravi Patel: that's fine — we can hand over an endpoint behind your ALB/NLB. we commonly front the runtime with NLB + TLS certs you manage via ACM. PrivateLink creates interface endpoints that are reachable via ENIs in your subnets and you control TLS termination.
[04:36] Priya Kumar: audit logs — we need request-level logs for 12 months. does Redwood ship application audit logs into our S3/bucket or do you store them?

[04:45] Maya Chen: in Private deployments we offer options: push logs to your S3 via our connectors, or deliver to your SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose. we can retain locally for a limited window but for compliance we recommend pushing to your retention bucket. we'll include examples in the runbook.
[05:02] Liam O'Connor: performance — if we run a model in eu-west-1, what's the expected tail latency for short prompts? also curious about batching and kv cache persistence across pods.

[05:12] Ravi Patel: typical p50 is sub-200ms for optimized models on dedicated GPUs, p95 depends on sequence length; our runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache pinning to reduce repeated context costs. for cross-AZ traffic, we'd recommend colocating the runtime with the EKS nodes that call it to avoid extra latency. for benchmarking we'd propose a short load test with your representative prompts.
[05:36] Ava Martinez: any blockers we've seen with customers moving from hosted to private?

[05:42] Maya Chen: common blockers are network diagram handoff delays and legal reviews. occasionally CIDR overlaps or corporate policy disallowing any outbound means we need an on-prem variant. we've done several customers with strict requirements by providing an air-gapped installer and on-prem runtime.
[06:00] Liam O'Connor: about auth between our services and the Redwood runtime — do you support mTLS, IAM, or token-based auth?

[06:08] Ravi Patel: support multiple: mTLS for service-to-service, AWS IAM sigv4 for certain integrations, and short-lived tokens for client SDKs. we can map to your identity patterns; SAML SSO is supported for console access.
[06:24] Priya Kumar: what about secrets and secret injection into containers? we need to ensure secrets don't get logged and are rotated frequently.

[06:31] Ravi Patel: we integrate with your Secrets Manager (AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault). secrets are mounted as ephemeral and not logged. rotation workflows are supported; we'll document best practices.
[06:45] Ava Martinez: regulatory note — EU personal data must remain in eu-west-1. if we replicate models for high availability, can you pin all EU traffic to eu-west-1?
[06:55] Maya Chen: yes, deployments can be pinned by region and routing rules will ensure EU requests land in eu-west-1. for user-level data residency we recommend separate deployments per region.
[07:06] Liam O'Connor: pricing question briefly — what's delta between Dedicated and Private? we like reserved capacity but want customer-managed network control.

[07:14] Maya Chen: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools managed by Redwood but still in Redwood VPCs; Private places runtime in your VPC and has different pricing (engineering/setup plus infra credits). we'll share a tailored estimate after we see your throughput profile. we'll include a pilot option for 3 months to test.
[07:30] Priya Kumar: competitor question — we've heard about Anthropic and OpenAI enterprise options. does Redwood support function/tool calling and streaming like those providers?
[07:40] Ravi Patel: yes — the API surface supports streaming, tool calling patterns, structured outputs. our differentiator here is deployment flexibility and observability for production workloads.
[07:50] Ava Martinez: ok sounds good. next up, what do you need from us to size this?

[07:55] Maya Chen: network CIDRs, expected RPS and token mix, target models, retention requirements, and any legal/Security contact for SOC2 review. you already mentioned most of these. if you can send the VPC diagram that will let ravi's team validate TGW/peering options.
[08:12] Liam O'Connor: we'll send that. one more technical: how do you handle updates/patches to the runtime? maintenance windows and notifications?

[08:20] Ravi Patel: for Private deployments we coordinate maintenance windows with you. patches are surfaced first in a staging cluster; we support canary rollouts and automatic rollback. we'll provide an SLA doc with patch cadence options.
[08:36] Priya Kumar: incident response — do you integrate with PagerDuty and provide runbooks?
[08:42] Maya Chen: yes, we integrate with PagerDuty and provide runbooks and playbooks. enterprise customers get a named CSM and 24/7 on-call options as an add-on.
[08:52] Ava Martinez: any gotchas with EKS? we host services in EKS and would like Redwood runtime to be reachable from pods without significant NAT overhead.

[08:59] Ravi Patel: common pattern is to attach the runtime into the same VPC and use internal LBs. if you have CNI restrictions, we can front with an NLB and use target groups. we will validate with your CNI details.
[09:14] Maya Chen: looks like we have clear action items. we'll send the runbook and sample network diagram; Ravi will schedule the infra deep dive. any final questions?
[09:22] Liam O'Connor: timeline — we're hoping to have a pilot in Q3. is that achievable?
[09:28] Maya Chen: absolutely, Q3 pilot is reasonable. once we get the network details and security review kickoff, we can provision a pilot environment within 2-4 weeks depending on calendar.
[09:36] Ava Martinez: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll circulate the docs internally and Liam will send CIDRs and topology by end of week.
[09:44] Maya Chen: thanks — we'll follow up with the runbook, security pack, and pricing. Ravi will reach out on scheduling the deep dive. talk soon.
[09:50] (call ends)
